items.readable_text:
Content:
A trigonometric identity is a relationship involving trigonometric functions that is always true!

Content:
Two of the most basic trigonometric identities are
[MATH: \tan \theta = \dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta},\qquad \cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}.]

Content:
These are identities, not equations, because they never give a false statement. We will always get equality, regardless of the value of [MATH: \theta] that we select (although it's important to note that [MATH: \theta] must lie within each function's domain).

Content:
In addition, we also have the two reciprocal relationships that we've already seen:
[MATH: \sec \theta = \dfrac 1 {\cos \theta},\qquad \csc \theta = \dfrac 1 {\sin \theta}.]

Content:
These reciprocal relationships are also trigonometric identities.

Content:
Trigonometric identities are useful when we want to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example of how this works.

items.title: Simplifying an Expression Using the Relationship Between Sine, Cosine, and Tangent

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall the identity [MATH: \tan \theta = \dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta},] and we substitute it into the given expression:

[MATH: \tan θ\cos θ|= (\sin θ)/(\cos θ) ⋅ \cos θ]

Now, we multiply the two quantities and simplify as much as possible:

[MATH: (\sin θ)/(\cos θ) ⋅ \cos θ|= (\sin θ ⋅ \cos θ)/(\cos θ); = (\sin θ ⋅ \cos θ)/(\cos θ); = (\sin θ)/(1); = \sin θ]

Therefore, [MATH: \tan \theta\cos\theta = \sin\theta.]

items.title: Rewriting a Trigonometric Equation Using an Identity

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall the identity [MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.]

To write the equation in terms of [MATH: \tan\theta] only, we divide both sides of the equation by [MATH: \cos\theta] and apply the above identity, as follows:

[MATH: 5\sin θ|= 2\cos θ; 5 ⋅ (\sin θ)/(\cos θ)|= 2 ⋅ (\cos θ)/(\cos θ); 5\tan θ|= 2]

Finally, we isolate [MATH: \tan\theta] by dividing both sides of the equation by [MATH: 5\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: (5\tan θ)/(5)|= (2)/(5); \tan θ|= (2)/(5)]

items.title: Simplifying a Complex Rational Expression Using Trigonometric Identities

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's interpret the fraction as a division:

[MATH: \dfrac {\cot \theta + \csc \theta} {\cos \theta + 1} = \left(\cot \theta + \csc \theta\right)\div \left(\cos \theta + 1\right)]

Then, we recall the identities [MATH: \cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}] and [MATH: \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},] and we substitute them into the above expression:

[MATH: (\cot θ + \csc θ) ÷ (\cos θ + 1)|= ((\cos θ)/(\sin θ) + (1)/(\sin θ)) ÷ (\cos θ + 1); = ((\cos θ + 1)/(\sin θ)) ÷ (\cos θ + 1)]

Finally, we turn the division into multiplication, and simplify the expression as much as possible:

[MATH: ((\cos θ + 1)/(\sin θ)) ÷ (\cos θ + 1)|= ((\cos θ + 1)/(\sin θ)) ⋅ ((1)/(\cos θ + 1)); = (\cos θ + 1)/(\sin θ(\cos θ + 1)); = ((\cos θ + 1))/(\sin θ(\cos θ + 1)); = (1)/(\sin θ); = \csc θ]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A trigonometric identity is a relationship involving trigonometric functions that is always true!

Content:
Two of the most basic trigonometric identities are
[MATH: \tan \theta = \dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta},\qquad \cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}.]

Content:
These are identities, not equations, because they never give a false statement. We will always get equality, regardless of the value of [MATH: \theta] that we select (although it's important to note that [MATH: \theta] must lie within each function's domain).

Content:
In addition, we also have the two reciprocal relationships that we've already seen:
[MATH: \sec \theta = \dfrac 1 {\cos \theta},\qquad \csc \theta = \dfrac 1 {\sin \theta}.]

Content:
These reciprocal relationships are also trigonometric identities.

Content:
Trigonometric identities are useful when we want to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example of how this works.

---

Item 2 — Example: Simplifying an Expression Using the Relationship Between Sine, Cosine, and Tangent

Example Prompt:
Simplify the expression [MATH: \tan \theta\cos\theta.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we recall the identity [MATH: \tan \theta = \dfrac {\sin \theta} {\cos \theta},] and we substitute it into the given expression:

[MATH: \tan θ\cos θ|= (\sin θ)/(\cos θ) ⋅ \cos θ]

Now, we multiply the two quantities and simplify as much as possible:

[MATH: (\sin θ)/(\cos θ) ⋅ \cos θ|= (\sin θ ⋅ \cos θ)/(\cos θ); = (\sin θ ⋅ \cos θ)/(\cos θ); = (\sin θ)/(1); = \sin θ]

Therefore, [MATH: \tan \theta\cos\theta = \sin\theta.]

---

Explanation:

[MATH: 3\cot θ\sin θ = 3 ⋅ (\cos θ)/(\sin θ) ⋅ \sin θ]

Then, we multiply the terms and simplify as much as possible:

[MATH: 3 ⋅ (\cos θ)/(\sin θ) ⋅ \sin θ|= (3\cos θ ⋅ \sin θ)/(\sin θ); = (3\cos θ ⋅ \sin θ)/(\sin θ); = (3\cos θ)/(1); = 3\cos θ]

Therefore, [MATH: 3\cot \theta\sin\theta = 3\cos\theta.]

Item 8 — Example: Rewriting a Trigonometric Equation Using an Identity

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: 5\sin\theta=2\cos\theta,] calculate [MATH: \tan\theta.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we recall the identity [MATH: \tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.]

To write the equation in terms of [MATH: \tan\theta] only, we divide both sides of the equation by [MATH: \cos\theta] and apply the above identity, as follows:

[MATH: 5\sin θ|= 2\cos θ; 5 ⋅ (\sin θ)/(\cos θ)|= 2 ⋅ (\cos θ)/(\cos θ); 5\tan θ|= 2]

Finally, we isolate [MATH: \tan\theta] by dividing both sides of the equation by [MATH: 5\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: (5\tan θ)/(5)|= (2)/(5); \tan θ|= (2)/(5)]

Item 11 — Example: Simplifying a Complex Rational Expression Using Trigonometric Identities

Example Prompt:
Simplify the trigonometric expression
[MATH: \dfrac {\cot \theta + \csc \theta} {\cos \theta + 1}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's interpret the fraction as a division:

[MATH: \dfrac {\cot \theta + \csc \theta} {\cos \theta + 1} = \left(\cot \theta + \csc \theta\right)\div \left(\cos \theta + 1\right)]

Then, we recall the identities [MATH: \cot \theta = \dfrac {\cos \theta} {\sin \theta}] and [MATH: \csc\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},] and we substitute them into the above expression:

[MATH: (\cot θ + \csc θ) ÷ (\cos θ + 1)|= ((\cos θ)/(\sin θ) + (1)/(\sin θ)) ÷ (\cos θ + 1); = ((\cos θ + 1)/(\sin θ)) ÷ (\cos θ + 1)]

Finally, we turn the division into multiplication, and simplify the expression as much as possible:

[MATH: ((\cos θ + 1)/(\sin θ)) ÷ (\cos θ + 1)|= ((\cos θ + 1)/(\sin θ)) ⋅ ((1)/(\cos θ + 1)); = (\cos θ + 1)/(\sin θ(\cos θ + 1)); = ((\cos θ + 1))/(\sin θ(\cos θ + 1)); = (1)/(\sin θ); = \csc θ]
